description:
What should parents most desire for their children? Beginning with Deuteronomy 6, Wesam Saad argues that the aim is wholehearted love for God. The command first addresses parents themselves, then requires them to teach their children diligently through ordinary family life. He contrasts that purpose with making education, wealth, comfort or physical wellbeing the highest measure of successful parenting. Costly faithfulness to Christ, rather than worldly security, supplies his controlling vision.

Colossians 3 and Ephesians 6 lead into the responsibilities of fathers. Saad interprets these passages as placing primary accountability for instruction and discipline on the father, while recognising the mother’s important help. His examples challenge fathers to remain involved when they return from work, instead of regarding spiritual teaching as a task permanently delegated to someone else.

The discussion also advocates physical discipline from selected Proverbs and explicitly rejects abuse and excess. Its final gospel illustration draws an essential distinction: outward correction cannot change selfishness or anger in the heart. Saad urges parents to begin with God’s goodness, explain wrongdoing in that setting and point children to Jesus as their only hope of inward change. Instruction is intended to reveal their need for a Saviour, not merely secure compliant behaviour.

questions.question: What parental purpose does Saad draw from Deuteronomy 6?
questions.answer: Parents are to love God with their whole being and teach that same wholehearted devotion to their children. Saad does not regard educational achievement, wealth, health or even outwardly respectable behaviour as an adequate replacement for that purpose. His aim is children who belong to Christ and live for Him.

questions.question: Why does the command begin with the parents’ own hearts?
questions.answer: The passage first calls the adults to love God with all their heart, soul and strength. Saad argues that parents cannot treat religious instruction as information passed on at a distance from their own lives. Their priorities, desires and example are part of what they teach.

questions.question: How is diligent teaching connected with ordinary family activities?
questions.answer: Sitting at home, travelling, resting and working all become settings for speaking about God. Saad reads the repeated situations and visible reminders in Deuteronomy 6 as a call to sustained instruction. The central truth is repeated in varied circumstances rather than confined to an occasional formal lesson.

questions.question: How are the father’s responsibility and the mother’s contribution distinguished?
questions.answer: Saad understands the commands addressed to fathers in Colossians 3 and Ephesians 6 as giving fathers primary accountability for their children’s instruction and discipline. He explicitly says that mothers also teach and help. Their contribution does not, in his argument, release fathers from personal involvement or justify permanently passing responsibility to them.

questions.question: How does Saad connect Ephesians 6:4 with neglecting a child’s instruction?
questions.answer: He places weight on the contrast between provoking children to anger and bringing them up in the Lord’s discipline and instruction. In his reading, neglecting that positive responsibility is itself a way of provoking them. He pairs the warning with Colossians’ concern that children should not lose heart and need encouragement.

questions.question: What role do the Proverbs play in the discussion of discipline?
questions.answer: Saad uses their language about the rod, correction and foolishness to argue for physical discipline as an expression of parental love. He also explicitly rejects abuse and excessive punishment. His later gospel illustration distinguishes this outward correction from the inward change that he says only Christ can bring.

questions.question: Why does the example begin with God’s goodness before addressing wrongdoing?
questions.answer: The child is reminded of God’s gifts and kindness before the parent discusses the angry or selfish response. Saad wants sin to be understood against that backdrop and the conversation to lead towards the need for Christ. The concern reaches beneath the incident to the desires of the heart, rather than ending with the visible behaviour.

questions.question: Why does the closing illustration say that discipline cannot change the heart?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes an outward consequence from the power to remove selfishness and anger. In the illustration, the instrument of correction cannot make the child gentle, even if punishment were repeated. He points instead to Jesus as the only hope for a changed heart, making the gospel the purpose of the conversation.
